steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement at the top of your file to import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the ES6 import syntax to import both React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react' here

// Your component code will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The file should have a proper import statement for React and useState, enabling you to use React components and state hooks.
successCriteria: import statement exists
imports React
imports useState from 'react'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing component state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but your import statement needs adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Import createSlice and createAsyncThunk from '@reduxjs/toolkit'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement to bring in createSlice and createAsyncThunk from the '@reduxjs/toolkit' package.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the named imports and the package path.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing from Redux Toolkit
import { createSlice, createAsyncThunk } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for createSlice and createAsyncThunk is added, making these functions available for use.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports createSlice and createAsyncThunk from '@reduxjs/toolkit'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported createSlice and createAsyncThunk from Redux Toolkit. These are essential for creating Redux slices and handling async logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement might be incomplete or have a typo. Make sure you're importing both createSlice and createAsyncThunk from '@reduxjs/toolkit'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import createSlice and createAsyncThunk from '@reduxjs/toolkit' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named App that returns null. Remember to include the return type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a functional component named App that returns null.
successCriteria: The code must define a component named App (function or arrow function) with a return statement that returns null, and include proper TypeScript return type annotation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a component named App that returns null and includes the correct TypeScript return type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named App that returns null with proper TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Define the initial state interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named CounterState to represent the shape of your Redux state. It should have three properties: count (number), loading (boolean), and error (string | null).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a CounterState interface that defines the structure for your Redux state with proper TypeScript types.
successCriteria: The interface should be named CounterState and include the three required properties with correct types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the CounterState interface with the correct property types. This will ensure type safety when working with your Redux state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface includes all three required properties (count, loading, error) with the correct TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. Make sure you're using the 'interface' keyword, naming it CounterState, and including count (number), loading (boolean), and error (string | null) properties.

steps.title: Create the initial state object
steps.instruction: Create an object named `initialCounterState` that matches the `CounterState` interface. It should have default values for all properties.
steps.hint: Define a constant object with the required properties from the interface. You can place it after the interface definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a properly typed initial state object that can be used as the starting point for your Redux slice.
successCriteria: The object is named `initialCounterState`
It has a type annotation `: CounterState`
It includes all required properties with default values
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the initial state object with proper typing and default values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your object includes all required properties from the interface and has the correct type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The initial state object is missing or doesn't match the CounterState interface. Make sure to create an object with all required properties and proper typing.

steps.title: Create an async thunk for incrementing after delay
steps.instruction: Create an async thunk named incrementAsync using createAsyncThunk. It should take no arguments, simulate a 1-second delay, then resolve with the number 1.
steps.hint: Use createAsyncThunk from '@reduxjs/toolkit'. The thunk should return a Promise that resolves with 1 after setTimeout.
steps.expectedOutcome: The incrementAsync thunk is defined and ready to be used in the slice.
successCriteria: Uses createAsyncThunk
Named incrementAsync
Returns Promise that resolves with number
Includes setTimeout or delay simulation
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created an async thunk that simulates a delayed increment operation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your thunk uses createAsyncThunk, is named incrementAsync, and returns a Promise that resolves with a number after a delay.
steps.feedbackWrong: The async thunk isn't quite right. Remember to use createAsyncThunk, name it incrementAsync, and have it return a Promise that resolves with a number after a delay.

steps.title: Create a slice with createSlice
steps.instruction: Create a counterSlice using createSlice with name, initialState, reducers, and extraReducers.
steps.hint: Use the createSlice function you imported earlier. Provide a name, initialState, reducers object, and extraReducers builder callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: A counterSlice variable is created using createSlice with the required configuration.
successCriteria: The slice must have a name property, an initialState property, a reducers object, and an extraReducers builder callback.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Redux slice with createSlice. This slice will manage your counter state and actions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your slice includes all required properties: name, initialState, reducers, and extraReducers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The slice wasn't created correctly. Remember to use createSlice with the required configuration properties.

steps.title: Initialize component state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, initialize a local state variable named 'count' using useState, starting with the value 0.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to provide the initial value (0) and destructure the returned array.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable with useState
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your App component will have a local state variable 'count' initialized to 0, ready to be used in the UI.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call inside the App component, destructuring into 'count' and its setter, with an initial value of 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state variable with useState. This gives your component local state that can be updated and displayed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure you're using useState inside the App component, destructuring into 'count' and its setter, and providing 0 as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count state variable wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use useState<number>(0) inside your App component and destructure the result into [count, setCount].

steps.title: Create a handler for synchronous increment
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function called handleIncrement that dispatches the increment action from counterSlice.actions.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls counterSlice.actions.increment() to get the action object.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleIncrement function that creates the increment action from your slice.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named handleIncrement that references counterSlice.actions.increment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a handler function that will dispatch the synchronous increment action.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named handleIncrement and calls counterSlice.actions.increment().
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a function called handleIncrement that uses counterSlice.actions.increment() to get the action object.

steps.title: Create a handler for asynchronous increment
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named handleIncrementAsync that dispatches the incrementAsync thunk.
steps.hint: Create an async handler function that calls incrementAsync() and dispatches it. Use the same pattern as your synchronous handler but with the async thunk.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleIncrementAsync function that dispatches the incrementAsync thunk when called.
successCriteria: The code must include a function named handleIncrementAsync that calls incrementAsync() and dispatches it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the async handler function. This will allow you to trigger the delayed increment action from your UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named handleIncrementAsync and properly dispatches the incrementAsync thunk.
steps.feedbackWrong: The async handler function is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a function named handleIncrementAsync that dispatches the incrementAsync thunk.

steps.title: Add JSX structure with buttons and display
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, return a JSX structure containing: a div wrapper, an h1 heading with text 'Redux Toolkit Counter', a paragraph to display the current count value, and two button elements (one for synchronous increment, one for asynchronous increment). Do not wire the buttons yet.
steps.hint: Use JSX syntax with a div, h1, p, and two button elements. The paragraph should show the count value from your component state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a JSX structure with a heading, paragraph showing count, and two buttons.
successCriteria: Return JSX with a div wrapper
Include an h1 with text 'Redux Toolkit Counter'
Include a paragraph element that displays the count value
Include two button elements with appropriate text
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the JSX structure with all required elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but some elements are missing or incorrect. Make sure you have: a div wrapper, h1 with 'Redux Toolkit Counter', paragraph showing count, and two buttons.
steps.feedbackWrong: The JSX structure doesn't match the requirements. Please add a div containing an h1, paragraph, and two buttons as specified.

steps.title: Wire buttons to their respective handlers
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's JSX return statement, add onClick handlers to both buttons. Connect the first button to handleIncrement and the second button to handleIncrementAsync.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on each button element and assign the appropriate handler function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The buttons will be interactive: clicking the first button immediately increases the count, and clicking the second button increases the count after a 1-second delay.
successCriteria: The first button has onClick={handleIncrement}
The second button has onClick={handleIncrementAsync}
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected both buttons to their respective handlers. The UI is now fully interactive.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some onClick handlers, but make sure both buttons are correctly wired. The first button should call handleIncrement, and the second should call handleIncrementAsync.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are not yet wired to their handlers. Add onClick attributes to both button elements, assigning the appropriate handler functions.
